headline: OpenAI reportedly wants all AI companies to give US government a 5% stake
summary: Sam Altman's proposal aims to clear political hurdles for AI development and share the benefits of the AI boom with the public through government equity.
details: OpenAI CEO Sam Altman is reportedly in talks with the US government to clear political hurdles for AI development. He has suggested a proposal where top AI companies, including OpenAI, Google, Anthropic, xAI, and Meta, would give the government a five percent stake in their businesses.
This proposal aims to share the benefits of the AI boom with the public. The idea comes as AI companies like Anthropic and OpenAI have faced government roadblocks when releasing new models.

For instance, Anthropic had to block access to its Mythos and Fable cybersecurity models after a Trump administration order, only recently regaining permission. OpenAI also rolled out a limited preview of its GPT-5.6 model to government-approved partners as requested.

In June, Trump signed an executive order asking AI companies to share their most powerful models for voluntary government review 30 days before public release. However, politicians and organizations like the UN are calling for even more stringent AI policies.

The Financial Times notes a precedent for government ownership, citing Intel. President Trump previously called for Intel CEO Lip-Bu Tan to resign until his administration took a 10 percent stake in the chipmaker.

Trump recently boasted that America's stake in Intel is now over $60 billion, up from $8.9 billion in 2025. Altman and other OpenAI executives reportedly floated the idea of giving equity to sovereign funds, such as the Alaska Permanent Fund.
These talks between OpenAI and the government are still in their very early stages. Any potential deal would require approval from Congress.

headline_marked: [[Google's webcam reCAPTCHA defeated]] by stock photo, asks for hand scan to prove you're human
headline: Google's webcam reCAPTCHA defeated by stock photo, asks for hand scan to prove you're human
summary: Google's experimental reCAPTCHA, which uses webcam hand gestures to verify users, was bypassed by testers using a static stock photo and a virtual camera, raising questions about its effectiveness.
details: Google is testing a new reCAPTCHA check that requires users to wave or hold up an open palm to their webcam, mapping 21 coordinates of the hand to verify a real person. This experimental method, part of Google Cloud Fraud Defense, was defeated within days by testers.

Testers bypassed the system by feeding a static stock photo of a hand through OBS Virtual Camera. This allowed them to pass the challenge without a live person, video, or AI involvement, simply by adjusting the image position.

The gesture check is designed to catch automated account creation and credential stuffing that older challenges miss. When triggered, it requests camera permission, records a brief video, and extracts hand-landmark data using its MediaPipe tools.

Google states that the footage is deleted after verification, no audio is recorded, and video is never tied to identity or shared. However, it also notes that data collected is used under the Google Privacy Policy, creating ambiguity about data handling.

The bypass highlights ongoing struggles for reCAPTCHA. In 2024, researchers achieved a 100% success rate against reCAPTCHAv2, and an OpenAI agent recently navigated Cloudflare's "I am not a robot" check. The hand-gesture test introduces biometric data, raising privacy stakes.

Major tech companies, including Google, Cloudflare, Mozilla, and Microsoft, recently proposed Private Access Control Tokens (PACT) as a cryptographic scheme to replace CAPTCHA challenges. This initiative aims to provide privacy-preserving proof of legitimate clients, addressing the rising bot traffic, which now accounts for 58% of global HTTP requests.
